description:
Somos estudiantes de geografía e ingeniería física del capítulo IEEE GRSS de la Universidad del Cauca. Unimos el análisis del territorio, la cartografía y los sistemas de información geográfica con la física, los datos y el desarrollo de software para crear una herramienta que acompañe al astronauta en su caminata por Marte, para avanzar seguro y hacer ciencia en cada paso. 

Si te gusta el espacio, los mapas o programar, aquí hay lugar para ti.
summary: MARSNOVA is an offline-first mobile app for the first astronauts who will explore the boxwork formations of Mount Sharp, in Gale Crater, on foot. It turns orbital data into decisions at human scale. From the HiRISE digital terrain model we built a 10 m terrain-cost matrix (slope, topographic position and roughness; slopes above 20° are blocked) and route the astronaut with A* along a real 3.7 km traverse with a base at its midpoint. At each science stop the astronaut answers Yes / No / Inconclusive to a field hypothesis; a Bayesian (Beta-Binomial) model updates the probability for all terrain of the same type and re-ranks the remaining stops by the information they can still provide, so the map learns from every observation. The app also brings Martian conditions into the walk: daylight, temperature, wind and dust from the Mars Climate Database, radiation dose from Curiosity's RAD, and solar-storm alerts from NASA DONKI, cached on the phone because a message to Earth can take up to 24 minutes. Everything works without a link to Earth and syncs without duplicates when the link returns.
details:
What it does

MARSNOVA is a layered map for an astronaut walking in a spacesuit through the boxwork ridges of lower Mount Sharp (Gale Crater, ~4.8° S, 137.3° E), the formations Curiosity began studying in 2025. It answers three questions during an EVA: where can I walk safely, where should I go next to learn the most, and are conditions safe to stay out.

How it works

1. Safe route: from the HiRISE DTM (1 m) our GIS analyst derived slope, topographic position index and roughness in QGIS and combined them into a 10 m relative cost matrix (1–6). Slopes above 20° are blocked, following NASA's Artemis walking-EVA concept by analogy. A* computes routes between stops; the planned 3.7 km route crosses three 10 m cells at 21.7–25.2°, which the app flags instead of forcing a 150–700 m detour. The base sits at the midpoint so the astronaut is never more than ~1.65 km from shelter.

2. Science that learns: five field hypotheses (fracture networks, hydrated minerals on ridges, shadows and line of sight, thermal behaviour, sedimentary contacts) start from a weak prior Beta(2,1) for each terrain type (ridge, hollow, sand). Yes adds to alpha, No to beta, Inconclusive changes nothing. Because one answer updates every cell of that terrain type, the whole map changes. The next stop is ranked by sum(science value × uncertainty) / (1 + route cost / 200), with a penalty for repeating a terrain type, and the app recommends returning to base when the remaining stops add little.

3. Conditions and alerts: Mars Climate Database v6.2 (temperature, pressure, wind, dust, sunlight; dust-storm scenarios) sets the best walking window; Curiosity RAD measurements set the walk dose and show what a solar event does (on May 20, 2024 radiation reached 55× background in 36 minutes); NASA DONKI provides space-weather alerts relayed from Earth and cached.

Evidence

We simulated 4,000 missions per walking budget on the real cost matrix (TypeScript, replicated in MATLAB). Up to 2 km both strategies choose the same stops; from 4 km the adaptive route calls hypotheses correctly more often (66–71% vs 60–69%) and ends with less uncertainty in 90–100% of missions.

Tools

React Native / Expo (TypeScript), Leaflet, SQLite (offline storage and sync queue), QGIS, JMARS, MATLAB, Python, Vitest.

Why it matters

Orbital data is abundant but regional; a person on foot needs route-specific, real-time decisions without waiting for Earth. MARSNOVA shows how open NASA data can become a field tool that keeps the astronaut safe and makes every observation count.
